subject: Biology
title: Sleep Stages and Cycles
description: A quick, practical guide to Sleep Stages and Cycles.

hook.text: Sleep isn't one state. Your brain cycles through distinct stages multiple times each night.

buildup.text: Stage 1 and 2 are light sleep. Stage 3 is deep slow-wave sleep—the most restorative phase.

discovery.text: REM sleep features rapid eye movements and vivid dreams. The brain is nearly as active as when awake.

twist.text: During REM, your body is temporarily paralyzed to stop you from acting out your dreams.

climax.text: A full night includes four to six cycles, each lasting about 90 minutes.

punchline.text: Your brain is busy all night. It just changes jobs.

quiz.question: Why is the body paralyzed during REM sleep?

details.summary: Sleep cycles through four stages roughly every 90 minutes: three stages of progressively deeper non-REM sleep followed by REM sleep. Each stage serves distinct functions including physical restoration, memory consolidation, immune function, and emotional processing.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding sleep architecture explains why interrupted sleep is not restorative even if total hours are adequate, and why different sleep disorders affect different stages with distinct consequences for health and cognition.
takeaways: Sleep cycles through NREM stages 1 through 3 and REM every 90 minutes
Deep NREM sleep dominates early night; REM dominates late night
Each stage serves distinct biological and cognitive functions

faq.question: Why is deep sleep so important?
faq.answer: Stage 3 NREM deep sleep is when growth hormone is released, immune function is enhanced, and declarative memories are consolidated. Missing deep sleep impairs physical recovery, weakens immunity, and reduces learning retention.

faq.question: Why do we get more REM sleep toward morning?
faq.answer: Sleep architecture shifts across the night. The brain prioritizes deep NREM restoration early when sleep pressure is highest, then shifts toward REM for emotional processing and procedural memory consolidation as physical restoration needs are met.
